Gravity. The fundamental force of attraction between all objects with mass. The weakest of the four known forces but dominant at cosmic scales. Isaac Newton quantified gravity mathematically in the seventeenth century through his law of universal gravitation. Albert Einstein reinterpreted it in the twentieth century as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy. Gravity governs planetary orbits, stellar structure, black holes, and the large-scale expansion of the universe.

Newton's law of universal gravitation states that force equals G times the product of two masses divided by the square of the distance between them. G is the gravitational constant, approximately six-point-six-seven times ten to the negative eleventh. Gravity is fundamentally an attractive force. There is no antigravity or gravitational repulsion. Masses always attract.

Gravitational acceleration at Earth's surface is approximately nine-point-eight meters per second squared, independent of an object's mass. All objects fall at the same rate in a vacuum, a principle Galileo discovered. Escape velocity is the minimum speed needed to leave a gravitational field permanently. For Earth, it is roughly eleven-point-two kilometers per second. For the Moon, it's about two-point-four kilometers per second.

Einstein's general relativity describes gravity not as a force but as the geometric curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy. Massive objects warp spacetime, and smaller objects follow geodesic paths. Tidal forces arise because gravity decreases with distance. The near side of an object experiences stronger gravitational pull than the far side, creating stress and deformation. Earth's ocean tides result from the Moon's gravity.

Black holes are objects so massive that their escape velocity exceeds the speed of light. Not even light can escape their event horizon. Gravitational lensing is the bending of light by gravitational fields, predicted by general relativity and observed in astronomical observations of distant galaxies. Mass is the source of gravitational attraction. More massive objects exert stronger gravitational forces. Gravity is one of the four fundamental forces, alongside electromagnetism, the weak force, and the strong force.
